used_clause:
An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ (Measurable spaces and measurable sets,
Probability measures and probability spaces). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
Law or distribution of a random element; it is a probability measure by
The law of a random element is a probability measure.

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.
premise_quotes: This is a finite statistical experiment: its parameter space is $(0,1)^E$ and its sampling law is the finite product of the stated receiver-outcome laws.

For $y\in\{0,1\}^{C_d}$ let
$$
\Omega_{d,y}=\left\{x\in\{0,1\}^{E_d}: y_r=\prod_{e\in P(o,r)}x_e\text{ for every }r\in C_d\right\},\qquad w_{p,d}(x)=\prod_{e\in E_d}p_e^{x_e}(1-p_e)^{1-x_e}.
$$
The one-probe outcome law is
$$
P_{p,d}(y)=\sum_{x\in\Omega_{d,y}}w_{p,d}(x).
$$
These probabilities sum to one because the sets $\Omega_{d,y}$ partition the finite link-state space and $\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{E_d}}w_{p,d}(x)=\prod_{e\in E_d}(p_e+(1-p_e))=1$. The complete experiment observes $N_d$ independent outcomes with law $P_{p,d}$ for each design, independently across designs. If the data are summarized by counts, $n_{d,y}\in\mathbb N_0$ is the number of probes in design $d$ with outcome $y$, and $\sum_y n_{d,y}=N_d$.

In a parametric model $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
two parameter values $\theta,\eta\in\Theta$ are **observationally
equivalent**, written $\theta\sim\eta$, if and only if
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta,
$$
that is, $P_\theta(A)=P_\eta(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). Equivalent parameter values therefore
give exactly the same sampling law. No distinctness of $\theta$ and $\eta$ is
required.

original_finding.location: ## Definition, the quoted formulation “Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function (Choice function).”
original_finding.evidence: “(Choice function)” is a citation-only parenthetical inside the complete axiom statement. The target is already linked in ## Definition references; remove the parenthetical without changing the axiom.

used_clause:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
premise_quotes: Assume AC for the library's standard-normal-law convention. Let a rooted tree have root $o$, one shared link $e_0=(o,v)$, and two branch links $e_1=(v,r_1)$ and $e_2=(v,r_2)$ to leaf receivers. On each probe, the three link delays are independent with laws $X_i\sim N(\mu_i,1)$, $i=0,1,2$, and the observed path delays are $Y_1=X_0+X_1$ and $Y_2=X_0+X_2$. The distinct link-mean vectors $\mu=(0,0,0)$ and $\mu'=(1,-1,-1)$ induce the same joint law of $(Y_1,Y_2)$; hence the three link means are not identifiable. The same equality holds for any number of independent repeated probes with these fixed link laws.
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC says every family of nonempty sets has a choice function; it is assumed here only because the cited normal-law definition declares it.

No stronger hidden measurable selector or countable-to-arbitrary choice inference occurs. The expanded family/domain membership formulation remains unambiguous despite the citation parenthetical. The finite coupling argument does not purport to prove AC.

used_clause:
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of sets, every member of which is nonempty. A
**choice function** for $\mathcal{F}$ is a function ([[def-function]])
$$g : \mathcal{F} \to \bigcup \mathcal{F} \qquad \text{such that} \qquad g(S) \in S \ \text{ for every } S \in \mathcal{F}.$$

Given a set $X$, a **choice function on $X$** means a choice function for the
family $\mathcal{P}(X) \setminus \{\emptyset\}$ ([[def-power-set]],
[[def-set-difference-and-symmetric-difference]]) of nonempty subsets of $X$.

original_finding.location: ## Definition, the sentence defining γ as a probability measure and the closing sentence identifying N(m,0).
original_finding.evidence: The definition inserts cited item titles as sentence fragments: “By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral ... is a measure” and “in The Dirac set function at a point”. Replace these fragments with mathematical prose and retain the links after the complete definition.

used_clause: Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.
premise_quotes: [F1] [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]: $N(\mu,1)$ is the pushforward of the standard normal law under $z\mapsto\mu+z$; the definition assumes AC.

1.1 On one probability space carrying independent $Z_0,Z_1,Z_2\sim N(0,1)$, set $X_i^{\mu}=\mu_i+Z_i$ and $X_i^{\mu'}=\mu_i'+Z_i$. By [F1], each vector has the required independent link-delay laws. [given, A1, F1, construct]

2.1 For $\mu=(0,0,0)$ the observation vector is $(Z_0+Z_1,Z_0+Z_2)$. For $\mu'=(1,-1,-1)$ it is $((1+Z_0)+(-1+Z_1),(1+Z_0)+(-1+Z_2))=(Z_0+Z_1,Z_0+Z_2)$. Thus the two observation vectors are equal on this coupling and have the same joint law; independent repetitions also have the same law. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

findings.soundness_explanation: The used normal-law clause is exactly N(μ,1)=law(μ+Z) for Z standard normal. On the finite product coupling, each shift preserves independence because each coordinate depends only on its own independent Z_i. The two observed sums agree pointwise after +1 and -1 cancel, giving the same joint law and repeated-probe products. No Gaussian convolution theorem, covariance-only characterization or zero-variance branch is needed. The existing grammar-only proposal retains AC, the probability-law construction, the affine pushforward formula and N(m,0)=Dirac_m. It therefore preserves this consumer interface. No duplicate normal-law proposal is created.

original_finding.location: ## Definition, the sentence ending “not inferred from separate likelihood-density versions (Likelihood densities)”.
original_finding.evidence: “(Likelihood densities)” is a citation-only parenthetical in the complete algorithm definition; its supplier link is already present in ## Definition references. Remove the parenthetical while retaining the logical clarification.

used_clause:
**Inputs.** Supply a measurable parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, sigma-finite measure spaces $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\nu)$ and $(\mathsf Z,\mathcal C,\mu)$, and a jointly measurable complete-data density $p(\theta,x,z)$ relative to $\nu\otimes\mu$ that integrates to one on each parameter fiber, as in Latent-variable joint and observed-data factorization. This joint measurability is supplied explicitly and is not inferred from separate likelihood-density versions (Likelihood densities). Also supply fixed observed data $x$, an initial value $\theta_0$, a mode `exact` or `generalized`, and a candidate selector that returns either a candidate or `unavailable` in finite time at each call. Require $0<m_{\theta_0}(x)<\infty$ and
$$\int q_{\theta_0}^x(z)\,|\log p(\theta_0,x,z)|\,\mu(dz)<\infty.$$

**Procedure.** For $t=0,1,2,\ldots$, check that $0<m_{\theta_t}(x)<\infty$; if not, return the current list with status `stopped: invalid current marginal`. Form $q_t$ and $Q(\cdot\mid\theta_t)$ on admissible candidates. If $Q(\theta_t\mid\theta_t)$ is not finite, return with status `stopped: current Q is not finite`. Call the supplied selector. In **exact mode**, its candidate set must consist of admissible candidates and contain $\theta_t$; it returns an attained maximizer of $Q$ on that set, or `unavailable` if no attained maximum is available. In **generalized mode**, it returns any admissible $\theta_{t+1}$ with $Q(\theta_{t+1}\mid\theta_t)\ge Q(\theta_t\mid\theta_t)$, or `unavailable` if no such update is supplied. If the selector returns `unavailable`, return with status `stopped: no required update supplied`; otherwise append its candidate and continue. The procedure asserts no convergence or global-optimality property and makes no assertion for a candidate that loses current latent support.
premise_quotes:
3. For each link $e$, compute its expected number of latent successes
$$
\widehat S_e^{(t)}=\sum_{d:e\in E_d}\sum_{y:n_{d,y}>0}n_{d,y}m_{e,d,y}(p^{(t)}).
$$
Set
$$
p_e^{(t+1)}=\widehat S_e^{(t)}/N_e\qquad(e\in E).
$$
This finite sum is the E-step conditional expectation of the complete-data success count; the displayed ratio is the M-step update instruction and lies in $[0,1]$ for each edge. Coordinates equal to $0$ or $1$ are allowed after an update.

All state sums are finite, and the finite link-state conditional probabilities are calculated directly; the generic measure-space/KL branch of the EM procedure is not invoked. The status records only the stopping rule that fired; it asserts neither parameter convergence nor a global optimum.
findings.soundness_explanation: The consumer uses finite latent-state conditional expectations and its explicit expected-count ratio M-step instruction. It expressly does not invoke the generic measure-space/KL branch and gives its own closed-cube extension and zero-likelihood stopping statuses. Thus this bounded interface does not infer joint measurability from separately chosen density versions, invoke the generic finite-KL branch at boundary points, or claim convergence/global optimality. The flagged likelihood-density parenthetical is citation text only. This is a contextual consistency review, not a proof of all generic EM hypotheses for every boundary iterate.
